content.text:
This lesson explores how global investment in the clean energy sector is shifting in response to the accelerating global energy transition. As countries work to decarbonize their economies, investments in clean energy technologies such as solar, wind and energy storage 💬️ have surged.
This lesson aims to show how capital flows have evolved in recent years and how clean energy is becoming a central pillar of the global energy mix.
Additionally, the lesson also wants to show regional disparities in investment, particularly between developed and developing countries, and the urgent need for more capital to meet global climate goals.
Ultimately, learners will gain insights into the key drivers and challenges influencing the global clean energy investments worldwide.

content.text:
Clean energy investment refers to capital flows directed toward technologies, infrastructure, and projects that reduce greenhouse gas emissions and support a transition to sustainable, low-carbon energy systems.

This technologies typically refer to:
Renewables (solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, bioenergy)
energy efficiency 💬️ (efficient buildings, appliances, industrial processes)
Electrification (electric vehicles, charging infrastructure)
Grids & storage (smart grids, transmission, batteries, storage solutions)
Emerging technologies (hydrogen and carbon capture)

The International Energy Agency defines clean energy investment as all investment going into low-emission power, grids, storage, energy efficiency, end-use electrification, low-emissions fuels, and other sustainable energy technologies (IEA, 2025).

The global clean energy landscape is undergoing a profound transformation, driven not only by the imperative to close the energy access gap, but more significantly by large-scale transitions in advanced economies such as the United States, the European Union, and China. This shift is motivated by the growing urgency to ensure sustainable, secure, modern and affordable energy systems .

In 2023, global clean energy investment reached USD 1.8 trillion and is projected to exceed USD 3 trillion in 2024, with nearly USD 2 trillion allocated to clean energy technologies and infrastructure (IEA, 2024). This marks a significant acceleration. Global investments in energy transition technologies rose by 19% compared to 2021 and nearly 70% compared to pre COVID-19 pandemic levels in 2019.
Global energy investment in 2024 is set to exceed

However, despite record-breaking levels of investments in clean energy, the world remains far from where it needs to be to stay on track for net-zero emissions by mid-century. The momentum is there but not yet ambitious or enough to reach the targets required.

To meet the goals that leaders set out in the Paris Agreement, annual investments in clean energy transition technologies must average 4.8 trillion between 2024 and 2030 (BNEF, 2024). As mentioned, the current investment levels, though impressive at over $3 trillion projected for 2024, still fall short, revealing a widening gap that must be urgently addressed. In 2023, USD $ 21.6 billion of international financial flows went to developing countries in support of clean energy (IEA, 2025)

At COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan in 2024, which was also known as the “Finance COP” world leaders acknowledged this gap and responded by raising the ambition of climate finance efforts. The international community committed to The New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) with a commitment to mobilizing USD $300 billion annually starting in 2025, tripling the previous USD $100 billion per year pledge made over a decade ago.

While this is a key step forward, the scale of the challenge demands even more coordinated action from governments, investors, and development institutions to reach the required investment gap.

metadata.title: Global Investment Gap for Clean Energy Investment

content.title: B: Geographical Disparities in Energy Investments

content.text:
While the world now is experiencing a strong momentum to accelerate energy investments, the Emerging Markets and Developing Economies (EMDEs) are in the most dire need of increased external investment in renewable energy in order to meet their SDGs and to transition to a more clean energy future.

According to UNCTAD and IEA, EMDEs need between $1.7 trillion and $2.8 trillion annually for clean energy investments each year in renewable and clean energy investments to cover the necessities such as solar PVs, wind, power grids and storage.

To meet this, annual investment must rise from $770 billion in 2022 to $2.2–2.8 trillion by the early 2030s. If China is excluded, the investment gap widens further, requiring annual investment to increase from USD 260 billion to as much as USD 1.4–1.9 trillion—a nearly sevenfold increase.

In 2024, EMDEs outside China account for only around 15% of global clean energy investment (IEA, 2024). Sub-Saharan Africa, for instance, received only 2% of the amount invested globally between 2000 and 2024 with most investments going to South Africa, Kenya, Uganda and Zambia.

The investment gap in renewable energy is also reflected in disparities of investment per capita across different regions. Clean energy investments are rising globally, but most of the growth is concentrated in a few countries and regions.

As per the previous graph shows there are the leaders in the clean energy investment namely, China, the U.S. and the European Union.

In the East Asia and the Pacific, China leads in investment and is set to spend almost $680 billion in 2024 (IEA, 2024). China is on track to meet - and in some cases exceed its clean energy targets as outlined in its 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-2025). This is thanks to a combinations of policy measures aiming to drive the clean energy growth such as:

Tax exemptions and subsidies which provide incentives in attracting investment and accelerate the deployment of solar and wind energy 💬️ projects
Infrastructure development focusing on power grid improvements and facilitating the integration of renewable energy sources
Introducing policies and regulatory reforms to encourage private sector participation and incentives in the renewable energy sector

Other countries in the region are also making big moves in the energy sector. For example, India is the third largest global investor in renewable and clean energy with over $60 billion investments in clean energy in 2024 (IEA, 2024)
Later on, in the lesson we will also highlight Indonesia’s role and potential in the region’s energy transition and investments. Another country is Thailand, that is aiming for 50% renewables in its power generation by 2050 (IEA, 2023)

In the United States, the energy-related provisions of the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), are expected to represent almost $870 billions of targeted support through 2031 in the form of tax credits, grants and loans, and investments in clean electricity, vehicle electrification, energy efficiency, carbon capture and storage 💬️ and low-carbon hydrogen. The US is the second-largest funding destination for energy transition technologies, with a total of $303 million spent in 2023 (BNEF, 2024) However, as of January 2025, the Trump Administration have suspended the IRA through an Executive Order and immediately paused the disbursement of funds appropriated through the IRA, although the vast majority of grants for clean energy programs appropriated under the IRA (Reuters, 2025)

In the EU, the European Commission's Green Deal Industrial Plan for the Net-Zero Age, introduced in February 2023 provides investment aid, simplified regulatory frameworks and tax breaks for net-zero product development, manufacturing, production, and installation in renewables and hydrogen sectors. The plan seeks EUR 225 billion in loans from the Recovery and Resilience Facility and EUR 20 billion in grants to support investments and reforms in the energy sector.
On the other hand, 120 emerging markets and developing countries receive little investment.

Clean energy investments in other countries flow predominantly to Brazil, Chile, and as mentioned India. Despite a global surge in clean energy investment, EMDE’s continue to receive a disproportionately small share of just 15% of the global clean energy investments, while they represent more than 50% of the world’s population.

In Africa, achieving the energy and climate-related goals by 2030 will require an annual investments of over $200 billion through the end of this decade. As the growing energy demand of the continent is growing and as it stands now the energy investments are equivalent to only 1.2% of the region’s GDP and clean energy investments, although increasing, account for just 2% of the global total (IEA, 2024)

In Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC), Brazil is leading the energy investments. In 2025, clean energy investment in LAC is projected to reach approximately USD 70 billion, marking a nearly 25% increase since 2015 (IEA, 2025). This growth underscores the region's commitment to expanding renewable energy infrastructure, despite facing diverse economic and political challenges.

In the Middle East, a region that is home to five of the world’s top oil producers: Saudi Arabia, Iraq, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Iran and Kuwait the energy investments in the region is expected to reach $175 billion in 2024, with clean energy accounting for around 15% if the total investment (IEA, 2024). However, the region’s power sector holds a huge potential for increasing investments in clean energy technologies, such as solar PV, and countries such as Saudi Arabia and UAE ambitions to diversify their economies towards other sectors away from oil to more sustainable and green sectors.

content.title: C: Triple Penalty of Energy Transition in Developing Country

content.text:
The "Triple Penalty" of the energy transition in EMDE’s refers to the three interrelated disadvantages: affordability, dependency and access that countries often are faced with in their energy transition efforts in shifting to clean energy:

Affordability:
EMDE’s typically face higher interest rates, higher financing costs and risk premiums, making clean energy projects more expensive to finance.
Dependence:
Many EMDE’s rely heavily on imported fossil fuels, making them vulnerable to price fluctuations, global conflicts and supply disruptions.
Lower Access to Technology and Skills:
Lack of access to advanced technologies, skilled labor, and innovation ecosystems, makes it harder for EMDE’s to deploy and operate clean energy infrastructure efficiently.

This triple penalties system creates a systemic disadvantage, exacerbating global energy inequality, risk countries to be stuck in fossil fuel/carbon lock-in and limiting the ability of these countries to meet their climate and development goals simultaneously. This multifaceted challenge hampers economic growth and exacerbates energy poverty.

metadata.title: Triple Penalty of Energy Transition in Developing Countries

content.text:
An increase in fossil fuel prices has significantly impacts households worldwide as a result of the energy crisis triggered by the war in Ukraine. Between February and September 2022, prices for coal and coal products surged by up to 235%, crude oil and petroleum products by up to 80%, and natural gas by up to 159%.

These hikes in energy prices directly translate to increased household energy costs globally, straining budgets significantly. Total per capita household energy costs increased by a range of 62.6% to 112.9% globally, leading to a 2.7–4.8% rise in household expenditure.

The distribution of these costs varies significantly across regions. For example in Central Asia households experiencing the largest direct increases in energy costs in Tajikistan, where direct energy costs soared by more than 176%. In Eastern Europe in October 2021, Moldova entered into an energy crisis when gas and electricity shortages caused tariffs to spike. In 2022, prices increased sevenfold for natural gas and 400% for electricity. As a result, ahead of winter 2022, more than 70% of the households in the country were deemed energy-vulnerable, spending more than 10% of their incomes on energy, in particular on heating during the cold period of November through March (UNDP, 2024).

Conversely, Latin American households were among the least directly affected, with increases around 51.5%. Additionally subsidies play a crucial role, for example in Venezuela energy prices are heavily subsidized. In contrast, the Caribbean region generally experiences higher energy costs.

A study focusing on electrifying all households in 40 Sub-Saharan African countries by 2030 highlighted several key aspects. The cost of electrifying these areas varies significantly depending on the level of service (Tier 2 to 4) with higher tiers necessitating greater capital. For instance, achieving Tier 3 levels of electrification results in average costs per person per day of USD16 cents, and for Tier 4, it escalates to USD40 cents per person per day (Researchgate, 2023). This presents a substantial challenge, particularly considering that around 429 million people mostly in Africa live below the poverty line (Statista, 2025)

Fossil fuels continue to play a dominant role in the global energy mix with data from 2022 - 2023 showing that approximately 80% of global primary energy still comes from coal, oil, and natural gas, especially in developing countries (IEA, 2024).

This reliance varies across regions, with some areas more dependent on specific types of fossil fuels for electricity production than others. For example, coal and gas are major sources of electricity globally, with oil contributing a smaller share.

The financial aspect of fossil fuel consumption is also significant. In 2022, global fossil fuel subsidies reached $7 trillion, or 7.1 percent of GDP (IMF, 2023). These subsidies are not only due to undercharging for supply costs but also for not accounting for the environmental and health costs associated with fossil fuel consumption. The majority of these subsidies arise from undercharging for the costs of global warming and local air pollution .

In 2023, governments – especially in emerging and developing economies – continued to heavily subsidies the use of fossil fuels, spending $620 billion (IEA)

Despite international climate agreements and growing awareness of the need for clean energy, the Production Gap Report 2023 highlights a concerning trend that governments plan to produce around 110% more fossil fuels by 2030 than would be consistent with limiting global warming to 1.5°C, and 69% more than would be consistent with a 2°C limit. This underscores a significant challenge in aligning national fossil fuel production plans with the global climate targets .

content.title: What should come before attracting more private sector investment in global renewable energy projects?

options.value: Establishing clear policy and regulatory frameworks
Increasing public awareness and community support
Securing initial grant or subsidy funding

takeaways.title: Investment in clean energy technologies is growing but remains insufficient to meet global climate targets Emerging Markets and Developing Economies (EMDEs) outside China account for only around 15% of global clean energy investment.

Significant investment disparities exist in the global energy transition China, the U.S. and the EU are leading the global energy transition race, while especially Sub-Saharan Africa is lagging significantly behind only receiving 2% of the amount invested globally in clean energy investments between 2000 and 2024, despite hosting over half of the world's population.

Regional disparities in energy transition investments highlight the need for equitable financing mechanisms. Many EMDE’s are facing the triple penalty of energy transition limiting their possibilities and creating a systemic disadvantage and increasing their risks to be stuck in fossil fuel/carbon lock-in and limiting their ability to meet their climate and sustainable development goals.
